gloss_terse: On account of, because of, for the sake of — causal preposition expressing reason or cause.
gloss_readable: Formed from the noun galal ('a weighty matter,' cf. Arabic jalal) with the prefixed preposition beth, this word functions as a causal connector meaning 'on account of' or 'for the sake of.' It appears in pivotal moments of blessing and judgment: God blessed Potiphar's house 'on account of Joseph' (Gen 39:5), and Moses was barred from the land 'because of you' (Deut 1:37). The multilingual evidence is remarkably uniform — English 'because-of,' Spanish 'por-causa-de,' French 'parce-que-de' — confirming a single, stable causal sense across all ten occurrences.

senses.1: A causal preposition meaning 'because of, on account of, for the sake of,' always formed as biglal (beth + galal). It introduces the reason or person responsible for a situation, whether positive — Laban recognizes blessing 'on account of' Jacob (Gen 30:27) — or negative — Israel will suffer 'because of' Manasseh's sins (Jer 15:4). All major translations converge on straightforward causal glosses, with no semantic variation across the ten attestations.

gloss_terse: Gerar — an ancient city in the Negev south of Gaza, prominent in the Abraham and Isaac narratives.
gloss_readable: Gerar was a Philistine city situated in the western Negev, traditionally identified with Tell Abu Hureirah south of Gaza. It features prominently in the patriarchal narratives: Abraham sojourned there under King Abimelech (Gen 20:1-2), and Isaac later settled in the same region, digging wells in the Wadi Gerar (Gen 26:17). The name appears with directional and prepositional forms — 'Gerar-ward' (Gen 10:19), 'in Gerar,' 'from Gerar' — but always denotes the same geographic location. Spanish 'Guerar' and French/German 'Gerar' preserve the toponym with minimal phonetic adaptation.

senses.1: The proper name of an ancient Philistine city in the Negev, south of Gaza, associated with the patriarchal sojourns of Abraham (Gen 20:1-2) and Isaac (Gen 26:1, 6). It also appears in the table of nations as a Canaanite border marker (Gen 10:19) and in Asa's military campaign (2 Chr 14:12-13). All ten occurrences refer to the same geographic site, with prepositional variants (in-Gerar, to-Gerar, from-Gerar) reflecting normal locative usage rather than distinct senses.

gloss_terse: Gittite — a gentilic adjective for an inhabitant of the Philistine city of Gath.
gloss_readable: This gentilic adjective identifies someone from Gath, one of the five Philistine city-states. It is applied to several notable figures: Obed-edom the Gittite, in whose house the ark rested (2 Sam 6:10-11); Ittai the Gittite, David's loyal foreign commander (2 Sam 15:19, 22); and Goliath of Gath (2 Sam 21:19). In its plural form with the article, 'the Gittites' designates the people of Gath collectively (Josh 13:3; 2 Sam 15:18). Spanish renders it 'el guitita,' while French and German maintain 'le/der Gittite,' all consistently pointing to Gath as the city of origin.

senses.1: A gentilic adjective meaning 'of Gath, belonging to Gath,' used to identify individuals or groups originating from the Philistine city of Gath. Applied in the singular to Obed-edom (2 Sam 6:10-11), Ittai (2 Sam 15:19, 22), and the giant slain by Elhanan (2 Sam 21:19), and in the plural to the Gittite contingent marching with David (2 Sam 15:18) or listed among the Philistine peoples (Josh 13:3). The consistent article usage (haggitti/haggittim) marks it as a well-recognized ethnic designation.

gloss_terse: Deborah — Hebrew proper name ('bee'), borne by Rebekah's nurse and by the prophetess-judge of Israel.
gloss_readable: The name Deborah, meaning 'bee' in Hebrew, belongs to two women in Scripture. The first is Rebekah's nurse, whose death and burial under the oak at Bethel is recorded in Genesis 35:8. Far more prominent is Deborah the prophetess, who judged Israel from her palm tree between Ramah and Bethel (Judg 4:4-5) and led the nation alongside Barak against Sisera's Canaanite forces. Her magnificent victory song in Judges 5 is one of the oldest poetic compositions in the Bible. The multilingual renderings — Spanish 'Débora,' French 'Débora/Devorah,' German 'Debora' — all preserve the name with minor phonetic variation.

senses.1: The proper name Deborah (Hebrew devorah, 'bee'), referring primarily to two figures: (1) Rebekah's beloved nurse, mourned at Bethel under the 'Oak of Weeping' (Gen 35:8), and (2) the prophetess and judge of Israel who summoned Barak to battle against Sisera (Judg 4:4-14) and celebrated the victory in the Song of Deborah (Judg 5:1, 7, 12). Eight of the ten occurrences belong to the prophetess. Translations across languages uniformly transliterate the name, confirming a single referential category.

gloss_terse: Dedan — a people and trading region in Arabia, descended from Cush (or Abraham through Keturah).
gloss_readable: Dedan appears in two genealogical lines: as a grandson of Cush through Raamah (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9) and as a grandson of Abraham through Keturah and Jokshan (Gen 25:3; 1 Chr 1:32). In the prophetic literature, Dedan is a prosperous Arabian trading community engaged in commerce with Tyre (Ezek 27:15, 20) and warned of coming judgment (Ezek 25:13; 38:13). The location is generally placed in northwestern Arabia along major caravan routes. Spanish 'Dedan,' French 'Dedan,' and German 'Dedan' all preserve the name identically, reflecting its stable identity as a geographic and ethnic designation.

senses.1: The proper name Dedan, denoting both a people and their territory in Arabia, traced genealogically to Cush via Raamah (Gen 10:7) and to Abraham via Keturah (Gen 25:3). Ezekiel portrays Dedan as a merchant power trading with Tyre in saddlecloths and precious goods (Ezek 27:15, 20), while also pronouncing judgment upon the region (Ezek 25:13). The pairing with Sheba (Ezek 38:13) places Dedan squarely within the Arabian commercial network. All ten occurrences refer to the same ethno-geographic entity.

gloss_terse: Darius — the Persian royal name borne by Darius Hystaspis, Darius Codomannus, and 'Darius the Mede.'
gloss_readable: This Old Persian name (Darayavaush, meaning 'he who holds firm the good') identifies up to three rulers in the Hebrew Bible. Darius I (Hystaspis, 522-486 BC) is the most frequently mentioned, appearing in Haggai, Zechariah, and Ezra as the king under whom the Second Temple was completed. Darius III (Codomannus, 336-330 BC) may be the Darius of Nehemiah 12:22. The enigmatic 'Darius the Mede' of Daniel 9:1 and 11:1 remains a subject of scholarly discussion. German renderings include the interesting prepositional forms 'fuer-Darius' and 'zu-Darius,' reflecting the genitive contexts in which the name frequently appears.

senses.1: The royal name Darius (Hebrew daryavesh, from Old Persian Darayavaush), applied to Persian-era kings. Most occurrences refer to Darius I Hystaspis, under whose reign the Jerusalem temple was rebuilt (Ezra 4:5; Hag 1:1, 15; Zech 1:1, 7). The name also designates Darius the Mede in Daniel (Dan 9:1; 11:1) and possibly Darius III in Nehemiah 12:22. The dating formula 'in the Xth year of Darius' is the characteristic syntactic frame, reflected in multilingual glosses like French 'Darius' and German 'zu-Darius.'

gloss_terse: Dathan — a Reubenite rebel who, with Abiram, challenged Moses' authority and was swallowed by the earth.
gloss_readable: Dathan, son of Eliab of the tribe of Reuben, is remembered as one of the principal rebels against Moses' leadership in the wilderness. Together with his brother Abiram and the Levite Korah, he challenged Moses' authority, famously refusing the summons with the defiant words 'We will not come up!' (Num 16:12). The dramatic divine judgment — the earth opening to swallow the rebels — is recalled in Deuteronomy 11:6 and celebrated in Psalm 106:17. The name is consistently transliterated across languages: Spanish 'Datan,' French 'Datan/Dathan,' German 'Datan,' confirming its singular referential identity.

senses.1: The proper name Dathan (Hebrew datan), identifying a Reubenite, son of Eliab, who together with Abiram led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Num 16:1, 12). All ten occurrences refer to this single individual across the Korah narrative (Num 16:1-27), the genealogical recap (Num 26:9), and later retrospective references (Deut 11:6; Ps 106:17). The name appears with conjunctions ('and-Dathan') and prepositions ('for-Dathan') but always designates the same person.

gloss_terse: Vashti — the Persian queen deposed by Ahasuerus (Xerxes) for refusing to appear at his banquet.
gloss_readable: Vashti (possibly from Old Persian vahista, 'best, most excellent') was the queen of the Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes I). Her story occupies the opening chapter of Esther: she hosted a parallel banquet for the women (Esth 1:9) and refused the king's command to display her beauty before his guests (Esth 1:12). This act of defiance set in motion the events that led to Esther's rise. The name is rendered consistently across translations — English 'Vashti,' Spanish 'Vasti,' French 'Vasthi,' German 'Waschti' — each adapting the Persian sibilants to local phonology while preserving the name's identity.

senses.1: The proper name Vashti, identifying the queen of Ahasuerus (Xerxes I) who was deposed after refusing the king's summons to his banquet (Esth 1:9-19). Her removal created the vacancy that Esther would fill (Esth 2:1, 4, 17). All ten occurrences are confined to Esther 1-2 and refer to this single individual. The phonetic variations across languages — Spanish 'Vasti,' French 'Vasthi,' German 'Waschti' — reflect different conventions for rendering the Persian consonant cluster.

gloss_terse: Ziph — a place name for towns in Judah (one near Hebron, one in the Negev) and a personal name in Chronicles.
gloss_readable: Ziph denotes at least two distinct locations and one person. The most prominent is the town in the hill country of Judah southeast of Hebron (Josh 15:55), whose surrounding wilderness became David's hiding place during Saul's pursuit (1 Sam 23:14-15; 26:2). A second Ziph is listed among the towns of the Judean Negev (Josh 15:24). The name also appears as a personal name — a son of Jehallelel in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 4:16). Rehoboam later fortified the Hebron-area Ziph (2 Chr 11:8). French preserves the toponym as 'Ziph,' while Spanish adapts it minimally to 'Zif.'

senses.1: The proper name Ziph, used for: (1) a town in the Judean hill country near Hebron (Josh 15:55; 2 Chr 11:8) and its associated wilderness where David took refuge from Saul (1 Sam 23:14-15, 24; 26:2); (2) a town in the Negev of Judah (Josh 15:24); and (3) a Judahite individual, son of Jehallelel (1 Chr 4:16). The directional form ziphah ('toward Ziph,' 1 Sam 23:24) and the construct midbar-ziph ('wilderness of Ziph') confirm the toponym's geographic productivity. All occurrences cluster around the single root identity.

gloss_terse: Zaccur / Zakkur — a Hebrew personal name ('remembered'), borne by several men from Reuben, Simeon, and Levi.
gloss_readable: The name Zakkur (meaning 'remembered' or 'mindful,' from the root zakhar) belongs to at least five different individuals in the Old Testament. The earliest is Zaccur son of Shammua, the Reubenite spy sent to scout Canaan (Num 13:4). Others include a Simeonite (1 Chr 4:26), several Levites — notably an Asaphite musician appointed by David (1 Chr 25:2, 10) and one who helped rebuild Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:2) — and a companion of Ezra (Ezra 8:14 Qere). The Septuagint renders it variously as Zakchhur, Zakchhour, reflecting the characteristic doubled kaph. German 'Sakkur' shows a distinctive adaptation of the initial sibilant.

senses.1: The Hebrew proper name Zakkur/Zaccur (from zakhar, 'to remember'), borne by multiple individuals: a Reubenite spy (Num 13:4), a Simeonite descendant (1 Chr 4:26), Levitical musicians and temple servants (1 Chr 24:27; 25:2, 10; Neh 10:12; 12:35), a wall-builder under Nehemiah (Neh 3:2), and a companion of Ezra (Ezra 8:14). Despite the variety of bearers, the name itself is morphologically consistent. Multilingual evidence — Spanish 'Zacur/Zakur,' French 'Zaccur,' German 'Sakkur/Zaccur' — shows standard transliteration patterns for this theophoric-adjacent name.
